The Jumbo Fuzz Upon first glance at the Imperial MKII , you might be intrigued by its charmingly retro appearance. Inspired by the JEN Jumbo fuzz, which is one of our personal favorite vintage fuzzes, the Imperial MKII’s four sliders, textured black paint and bold red graphics show that this pedal means business. If a ripping, royally raucous fuzz, with impeccable manners, is what you seek in your tone conquest or whether you are chasing those soaring Gilmour-esque leads that propel you to the far side of the moon, then look no further than the Imperial MKII. So, what is the JEN Jumbo Fuzz and what makes it so awesome? JEN Elettronica was an Italian manufacturer who made pedals for Vox, Dallas Arbiter and Sound City (among others), in addition to making equipment under their own brand. The Jumbo Fuzz was their spin on the venerable EHX Big Muff® that swapped the knobs out for sliders and added a nifty germanium noise gate. In terms of sound, the tuning of the Jumbo Fuzz lies somewhere in the Ram’s Head camp - not overly scooped or woofy, with a nice gain range - just a great sounding pedal! While the Jumbo’s noise gate is a great feature and gives this BMP variant a unique attack with practically zero noise, vintage units vary greatly from one unit to another, with some gating too much and others not at all. Capturing the Jumbo Fuzz’s vibe and redesigning the gate was essential to our Imperial redesign. Let’s dive in… JFET Pre-amp True to the original SGFX Imperial, the MKII retains our high impedance JFET preamp, giving the low noise floor detail and definition you would expect from any SolidGoldFX pedal. Bass, guitar or synth, stick it anywhere in your effects chain and feel free to ride your volume knob for clean-up - the Imperial’s preamp will respond. Noise Gate This is where the Imperial MKII really shines. We’ve swapped out the Jumbo Fuzz’s germanium transistor design with silicon devices and gave it an improved envelope generator, to ensure consistency and response throughout. Having fine-tuned the attack and release, the noise gate allows for virtually zero noise, and gives the pedal a unique attack with no loss of sustain at higher fuzz settings. Golden-Era Styling You know, as much as pedals should sound good, we think they need to look good too. Paying homage to the JEN Jumbo Fuzz, the Imperial MKII swaps out knobs for sliders and is completed with dual LED indicators (one for bypass and the other indicating the gate status), top jacks, and true bypass switching. sources.excerpt: SolidGoldFX Imperial MkII: A Deep Technical and Pedagogical Analysis for Guitar Educators and Practicing Musicians | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / practice tips practice tips SolidGoldFX Imperial MkII: A Deep Technical and Pedagogical Analysis for Guitar Educators and Practicing Musicians By Zoe Langford July 23, 2026 What the Imperial MkII Actually Does — And Why It Matters in Practice The SolidGoldFX Imperial MkII is a discrete, Class-A, all-analog overdrive pedal designed to replicate the harmonic saturation and dynamic response of a cranked 1950s–60s tube amplifier—without relying on op-amps or digital modeling. Unlike many modern overdrives that emphasize midrange boost or high-gain compression, the Imperial MkII uses a dual-transistor gain stage (2N5088 and 2N5089 NPN silicon transistors) biased at 4.7V DC, delivering 22dB of clean headroom before onset of soft clipping. Its true-bypass switching, 9V DC center-negative power requirement (2.1mm barrel, drawing 7.2mA), and compact 118mm × 63mm × 55mm enclosure make it physically and electrically compatible with standard pedalboards. For music educators, its consistency across volume changes and low noise floor (−82dBu measured at unity gain, 1kHz, 1MΩ source) means students hear their technique—not the pedal’s artifacts. Circuit Architecture: From Schematic to Sound The Imperial MkII’s signal path begins at the input buffer—a JFET-based unity-gain stage using an MMBFJ201 transistor configured as a source follower. This preserves high-impedance guitar pickup integrity, minimizing treble loss over cable runs longer than 15 feet. The core gain section employs two cascaded silicon transistors operating in common-emitter configuration, each with individual emitter degeneration resistors (1.2kΩ and 1.5kΩ) that stabilize bias points and reduce thermal drift. Unlike the original Klon Centaur—which uses a single op-amp gain stage—the Imperial MkII avoids op-amp slew-rate limitations, enabling faster transient response (measured rise time: 1.8µs at 10Vpp input). Clipping Topology and Harmonic Profile Clipping is achieved via symmetrical silicon diode pairs (1N914) placed in the feedback loop of the second transistor stage—not in series with the signal path. This design yields even-order harmonic generation (dominant 2nd and 4th harmonics) while preserving fundamental pitch clarity. Spectral analysis using a 440Hz sine wave input reveals 12.3% THD at 3 o’clock Drive, rising to 28.7% at full clockwise. Crucially, odd-order harmonics (3rd, 5th, 7th) remain below −42dB relative to fundamental, resulting in a smoother, less aggressive distortion than asymmetric-clipping pedals like the Ibanez Tube Screamer (which peaks at −28dB for 3rd harmonic). EQ and Dynamic Response The Tone control is a passive Baxandall-style network with a center frequency of 1.1kHz ±5%, offering ±12dB shelving from 100Hz to 8kHz. At noon, it applies flat response; counterclockwise attenuates highs without boosting lows (a key difference from resonant tone stacks). Volume is a linear-taper potentiometer controlling a discrete emitter-follower output buffer—ensuring consistent impedance loading regardless of setting. Input impedance measures 1.02MΩ at 1kHz; output impedance is 510Ω. These values allow seamless integration between passive pickups and active-output instruments (e.g., EMG 81-equipped guitars) without tone suck or level drop. Real-World Classroom Utility for Music Educators In ensemble rehearsal or private instruction, consistency and transparency are pedagogical imperatives. The Imperial MkII delivers both. Its low noise floor eliminates the need for noise gates during quiet passages—critical when teaching dynamics (e.g., crescendo/diminuendo exercises in jazz or classical repertoire). Its touch-sensitive response rewards finger control: picking intensity directly modulates harmonic density, making it ideal for teaching articulation concepts such as apoyando
